directions: Plant a container or balled-and-burlapped tree in full sun in well-drained soil in spring or fall; this U.S. National Arboretum hybrid, a 1971 cross of European field elm and Chinese elm released in 1990, was bred specifically to combine strong Dutch elm disease tolerance with a compact size suited to street tree plantings and spaces beneath power lines. It grows into a stiff, upright-pyramidal form with small, glossy leaves that turn an unusual reddish-purple in fall, a rare color break among elms. Little pruning is needed beyond early structural training to establish a dominant leader, and the tree tolerates urban soils and pollution well. Because it sets very little viable seed, it also avoids the litter problems common to many elms.

Plant a container or balled-and-burlapped tree in full sun in average, well-drained soil in spring; selected in 1975 from Wilson elm seedlings at the USDA station in Delaware, Ohio and released without patent in 1990, 'Prospector' offers excellent resistance to Dutch elm disease and elm leaf beetle in a fast-growing shade tree that recalls the classic vase shape of American elm. New leaves emerge with an orange-red flush before maturing to dark green and turning bright yellow in fall. Because it grows quickly and can produce narrow branch angles, plan on formative pruning in the first several years to build strong scaffold branching.

Plant in full sun in well-drained soil in spring, staking young trees if needed to encourage a single dominant leader; this Manitoba-bred selection, chosen in 1985 from seedlings grown at Treherne from Morden Research Station stock, is prized on the Canadian prairies for combining strong Dutch elm disease resistance with exceptional cold hardiness. It forms a symmetrical, upright vase shape with dark green foliage and good drought tolerance once established. Prune in the early years to correct any co-dominant leaders, since uncorrected forks can weaken the crown as the tree matures.

Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in spring, and keep roots consistently cool and moist with mulch since birches are shallow-rooted; this cultivar, selected by nurseryman Tom Pinney Jr. for straight trunks and a strong upright-pyramidal habit, is notable for resisting the bronze birch borer that devastates many paper birches planted south of their native range. Brilliant white bark begins peeling in curling layers while trees are still young, and the bright green summer foliage turns golden yellow in fall. It tolerates heat better than typical paper birch seedlings, extending the species' usable range into warmer zones, but still performs best with protection from prolonged drought and compacted soil.

Plant in full sun to light shade in medium to consistently moist, well-drained soil in spring, mulching to keep roots cool as with all birches; one of the oldest and most widely planted Himalayan birch selections, 'Doorenbos' is valued for chalky white bark that whitens further with age and peels away from young trunks and branches almost immediately, unlike many seed-grown jacquemontii that take years to color up. Its vigorous, oval-crowned form carries glossy dark green leaves that turn gold in autumn, and yellowish-brown catkins appear in spring. It has earned the Royal Horticultural Society's Award of Garden Merit for its reliable ornamental bark and low-maintenance habit.

Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil in spring; this smaller, less common relative of Japanese zelkova is grown chiefly for its exfoliating bark, which develops a mosaic of gray, orange, and rich brown patches on mature trunks for outstanding winter interest. It stays considerably more compact than Zelkova serrata, often developing multiple trunks, with glossy dark green leaves that turn a muted brownish yellow in fall. Highly adaptable to heavy clay and varied soil conditions and tolerant of drought once established, it makes a good specimen tree for a smaller residential lot where a full-size zelkova would outgrow the space. Provide it with the open, sunny site it needs to develop its best branching structure.
sources: Trees and Shrubs Online (International Dendrology Society)

directions: Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, well-drained soil in spring; this narrower, more upright selection of littleleaf linden tops out around 50 feet, noticeably smaller and more formal in outline than the straight species, and is well suited to street tree plantings where a compact pyramidal crown is an asset. Fragrant cream and yellow flowers appear in early summer and are a magnet for bees, while dark green summer foliage turns a soft yellow in fall. Its tighter branching gives it somewhat better resistance to storm damage than wide-spreading lindens, though it still benefits from deep, infrequent watering during establishment and dry spells.

Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil in spring; this vigorous, symmetrical selection of silver linden forms a dense pyramidal canopy of dark green leaves with silvery-white undersides that flash attractively whenever a breeze moves through them. Small, fragrant, cream-white flowers in early summer draw heavy pollinator traffic, and the tree tolerates city heat, pollution, and drier soils notably better than littleleaf or American linden once established. Reported resistance to Japanese beetle and gypsy moth feeding, along with good verticillium wilt tolerance, makes it a durable choice for streets and parking lot islands where many shade trees struggle.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in fertile, well-drained soil in spring; this old, uncommon European hornbeam selection is grown for its deeply and irregularly cut, jaggedly toothed leaves, which give the canopy a fine, lacy texture reminiscent of a fern frond rather than the smooth-edged foliage of the species. Growth is slow and the crown tends toward a looser, more open, irregular shape than typical hornbeam cultivars, so occasional shaping helps develop a pleasing form over time. Otherwise it shares the species' tough constitution, tolerating heavy clay, urban pollution, and the same wide pH range, and its toothed leaves turn yellow before falling in autumn.

Plant in full sun to dappled shade in evenly moist, well-drained soil in spring; discovered as a wild seedling in Waukesha County, Wisconsin, this compact selection of American hornbeam matures into a dense, rounded globe form only about 15 feet tall and wide, far more uniform and predictable than the irregular, multi-stemmed shape typical of seed-grown native hornbeam. Its standout feature is reliable orange-red fall color, a step up from the variable yellow-to-red fall display of the species. Slow growing and adaptable to a wide range of soils from clay to rich loam, it fits well into smaller gardens or as a uniform specimen where the wide-spreading straight species would be too large.

Plant in full sun to partial shade in moist, acidic, well-drained soil in spring, since black tupelo develops a deep taproot and transplants best while young; this vigorous selection forms a neatly conical crown and carries glossier, thicker-textured leaves than typical seedlings, which shows increased resistance to leaf spot diseases that can mar tupelo foliage late in the season. Its main draw is exceptionally reliable, brilliant scarlet-red fall color displayed uniformly across the whole canopy, arriving earlier and more consistently than on straight-species trees. Like other tupelos it tolerates both wet bottomland soils and average garden conditions once established, and its flowers are an excellent early-season nectar source for bees.

Plant in full sun in moist, well-drained, slightly acidic soil in spring; this cultivar solves sweetgum's biggest landscape drawback by setting essentially no spiny seed pods, eliminating the litter and bare-foot hazard that keeps many homeowners from planting the species. It grows into a narrower, sturdier pyramid than seed-grown sweetgum, with new foliage emerging with a maroon blush before turning glossy green, then finishing fall in a mix of yellow, orange, red, and purple often on the same leaf. Because it still forms a dense, structurally strong canopy at a moderate size, it requires little pruning and makes a low-maintenance shade or street tree once established.
